claim: In both Drosophila and mammals, the brain contains the most diverse population of cell types of any tissue.
source: In both Drosophila and mammals, the brain contains the most diverse population of cell types of any tissue.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain cellular diversity that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Transcriptional diversity is an early step in generating neuronal and glial diversity.
source: It is generally accepted that transcriptional diversity is an early step in generating neuronal and glial diversity, followed by the establishment of a unique gene expression profile that determines morphology, connectivity, and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by general scientific consensus in the field of developmental neuroscience.

claim: In Drosophila, there are two types of neural stem cells, called Type 1 (T1) and Type 2 (T2) neuroblasts.
source: In Drosophila, there are two types of neural stem cells, called Type 1 (T1) and Type 2 (T2) neuroblasts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neural stem cell types.

claim: The diversity of T2-derived neurons contributes a large portion of the central complex (CX).
source: The diversity of T2-derived neurons contributes a large portion of the central complex (CX), a conserved brain region that plays a role in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about T2 neuroblast contributions to the central complex.

claim: The central complex is a conserved brain region that plays a role in sensorimotor integration.
source: The diversity of T2-derived neurons contributes a large portion of the central complex (CX), a conserved brain region that plays a role in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the central complex.

claim: The study performed single nuclei RNA sequencing of T2 neuroblast-derived adult neurons and glia.
source: Here we perform single nuclei RNA sequencing of T2 neuroblast-derived adult neurons and glia.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study identified clusters containing all known classes of glia.
source: We identify clusters containing all known classes of glia, clusters that are male/female enriched, and 161 neuron-specific clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The study identified 161 neuron-specific clusters.
source: We identify clusters containing all known classes of glia, clusters that are male/female enriched, and 161 neuron-specific clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the clustering analysis of the snRNA-seq data.

claim: The study identified clusters that are male/female enriched.
source: We identify clusters containing all known classes of glia, clusters that are male/female enriched, and 161 neuron-specific clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-specific analysis of the snRNA-seq data.

claim: Each cluster has a unique transcription factor combinatorial code.
source: We map neurotransmitter and neuropeptide expression and identify unique transcription factor combinatorial codes for each cluster.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis across clusters.

claim: Several columnar neuron subtypes map to distinct clusters.
source: We map several columnar neuron subtypes to distinct clusters and identify two neuronal classes (NPF+ and AstA+) that both map to two closely related clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuron-to-cluster mapping analysis.

claim: NPF+ and AstA+ neurons both map to two closely related clusters.
source: We map several columnar neuron subtypes to distinct clusters and identify two neuronal classes (NPF+ and AstA+) that both map to two closely related clusters.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the neuropeptide expression and cluster mapping analysis.

claim: Each transcriptional cluster represents one or a few closely related neuron subtypes.
source: Our data support the hypothesis that each transcriptional cluster represents one or a few closely related neuron subtypes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the cluster analysis and neuron mapping results.

claim: The laterally positioned optic lobes have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia.
source: In Drosophila, the laterally positioned optic lobes have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia (Konstantinides et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2022; Özel et al., 2022), as has the central brain and ventral nerve cord (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2021; Naidu et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2021; Sato and Suzuki, 2022; Shu et al., 2023; Velten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The central brain and ventral nerve cord have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia.
source: In Drosophila, the laterally positioned optic lobes have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia (Konstantinides et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2022; Özel et al., 2022), as has the central brain and ventral nerve cord (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2021; Naidu et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2021; Sato and Suzuki, 2022; Shu et al., 2023; Velten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The mushroom body (MB) is used for learning and memory.
source: The central brain contains many diverse neurons that populate important neuropils, such as the mushroom body (MB) used for learning and memory (Sgammeglia and Sprecher, 2022), or the central complex (CX) used for celestial navigation and sensory-motor integration (Fisher, 2022), among other behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The central complex (CX) is used for celestial navigation and sensory-motor integration.
source: The central brain contains many diverse neurons that populate important neuropils, such as the mushroom body (MB) used for learning and memory (Sgammeglia and Sprecher, 2022), or the central complex (CX) used for celestial navigation and sensory-motor integration (Fisher, 2022), among other behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: T1 NBs undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate a series of ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which each produce two post-mitotic neurons.
source: T1 NBs undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate a series of ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which each produce two post-mitotic neurons (Pollington et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There are ~100 T1 NBs per larval central brain lobe that each generate 20–100 neurons and glia.
source: There are ~100 T1 NBs per larval central brain lobe that each generate 20–100 neurons and glia (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T2 NBs undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and generate an intermediate neural progenitor (INP).
source: T2 NBs undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and generate an intermediate neural progenitor (INP); each INP undergoes 4–6 divisions to self-renew and generate a GMC and its two neuron or glial progeny (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Each INP undergoes 4–6 divisions to self-renew and generate a GMC and its two neuron or glial progeny.
source: T2 NBs undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and generate an intermediate neural progenitor (INP); each INP undergoes 4–6 divisions to self-renew and generate a GMC and its two neuron or glial progeny (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Each T2 NB division will generate 8–12 progeny cells.
source: Thus, each T2 NB division will generate 8–12 progeny cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about INP divisions producing 4-6 GMCs, each producing 2 progeny.

claim: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons.
source: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons (Yu et al., 2013), have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), and produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX (Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: T2 NBs have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity.
source: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons (Yu et al., 2013), have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), and produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX (Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T2 NBs produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX.
source: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons (Yu et al., 2013), have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), and produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX (Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) has been done on adult central brain neurons and glia.
source: Although single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) has been done on adult central brain neurons and glia (Croset et al., 2018), the transcriptomic profile of T1 versus T2 neuronal and glial progeny has not yet been characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The transcriptomic profile of T1 versus T2 neuronal and glial progeny has not yet been characterized.
source: Although single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) has been done on adult central brain neurons and glia (Croset et al., 2018), the transcriptomic profile of T1 versus T2 neuronal and glial progeny has not yet been characterized.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Focused transcriptional profiling of T2-derived progeny has not been reported.
source: Furthermore, the T2 lineages generate diverse neuronal progeny (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013) but focused transcriptional profiling of T2-derived progeny has not been reported.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The study sequenced a total of 30,699 nuclei at 589 median genes per nuclei from the T1+T2 central brain.
source: We sequenced a total of 30,699 nuclei at 589 median genes per nuclei from the T1+T2 central brain.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing experiment.

claim: 3,125 nuclei were assigned as being derived from T2 lineages based on expression of RFP, GFP, or FLP.
source: We assigned 3,125 nuclei which have expression of RFP, GFP, or FLP as being derived from T2 lineages.
evidence: This describes the method used to identify T2-derived nuclei in the dataset.

claim: 27,574 triple-negative nuclei were assigned as derived from the T1 lineages.
source: We assigned 27,574 triple-negative nuclei as derived from the T1 lineages.
evidence: This describes the method used to identify T1-derived nuclei in the dataset.

claim: The UMAP was generated with 152 clusters.
source: We used uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)-based dimension reduction to visualize the 152 clusters (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis, also shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both T1 and T2 generate transcriptionally similar cells, despite their different developmental origins.
source: We conclude that both T1 and T2 generate transcriptionally similar cells, despite their different developmental origins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that no cluster exclusively contained progeny from T1 or T2 NB lineages.

claim: T2 enriched clusters show high expression of AstA (Allatostatin A), SerT (Serotonin transporter), Tk (Tachykinin), and Vmat (Vesicular monoamine transporter).
source: We next searched for cluster-defining genes in the T2 enriched clusters (Figure 1C') and found high expression of AstA (Allatostatin A), SerT (Serotonin transporter), Tk (Tachykinin), and Vmat (Vesicular monoamine transporter) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AstA+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, and TK+ neurons may be primarily derived from T2 lineages.
source: These enriched marker genes suggest that AstA+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, and TK+ neurons may be primarily derived from T2 lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of specific marker genes in T2 clusters.

claim: The study identified 3409 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan-glial marker repo in the T1+T2 atlas.
source: We focused on the 3409 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan-glial marker repo (Campbell et al., 1994; Xiong et al., 1994) in the T1+T2 atlas (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the glial cell analysis, with citations supporting repo as a pan-glial marker.

claim: Each glial cluster contained a mix of T1 and T2 glial progeny.
source: Each cluster contained a mix of T1 and T2 glial progeny (Figure 1E').
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1E'.

claim: The study identified six known glial cell types: astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, surface glial and the two subtypes: perineurial and subperineurial.
source: We identified six known glial cell types (astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, surface glial and the two subtypes: perineurial and subperineurial) based on canonical glial makers (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the glial cell type identification analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Some glial subtypes (astrocytes, ensheathing, and subperineurial) map to multiple clusters.
source: Similar to a previous glial cell atlas (Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023), we found some glial subtypes (astrocytes, ensheathing, and subperineurial) mapping to multiple clusters (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 1E and F, with a citation to a previous study showing similar results.

claim: A glial cluster expressed genes associated with extracellular matrix, vkg and Col4a1.
source: We identified a glial cluster that expressed genes associated with extracellular matrix, vkg and Col4a1 (Figure 1F), which have previously been identified as pan surface glial markers (DeSalvo et al., 2014; Hindle and Bainton, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1F, with citations supporting these genes as surface glial markers.

claim: The two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial clusters, do not express vkg and Col4a1 at cluster defining levels.
source: Interestingly, the two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial clusters, do not express these markers at cluster defining levels, and conversely the surface glia cluster 5 does not express perineurial or subperineurial specific makers (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the gene expression data shown in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis for all genes between T1 and T2 glial progeny did not show differences across any glial cell types or clusters.
source: Differential gene expression analysis for all genes between T1 and T2 glial progeny did not show differences across any glial cell types or clusters (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a result from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The T1 neuron atlas contains 22,807 T1-derived neurons that form 114 clusters.
source: We then generated a T1 neuron atlas containing 22,807 T1-derived neurons that form 114 clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T1 neuron atlas generation.

claim: The study sequenced 61,118 T2 nuclei.
source: In total, we sequenced 61,118 T2 nuclei.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T2-specific sequencing experiment.

claim: The T2 atlas contains 64,243 nuclei that formed 198 clusters.
source: We used integration in Seurat to generate an atlas containing 64,243 nuclei that formed 198 clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the integrated T2 atlas generation.

claim: T2 NBs have been estimated to produce ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain.
source: T2 NBs have been estimated to produced ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013), with ~1800 neurons in the central complex (Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024), giving our atlas ~12 x coverage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T2 NBs produce ~1800 neurons in the central complex.
source: T2 NBs have been estimated to produced ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013), with ~1800 neurons in the central complex (Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024), giving our atlas ~12 x coverage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The T2 atlas has ~12 x coverage of T2-derived neurons.
source: T2 NBs have been estimated to produced ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013), with ~1800 neurons in the central complex (Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024), giving our atlas ~12 x coverage.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of sequenced nuclei relative to the estimated total number of T2-derived neurons.

claim: The T2 neuron cell atlas contains 50,148 non-glial nuclei forming 161 clusters.
source: We next filtered out the repo+ glial cell clusters to generate a T2 neuron cell atlas with 50,148 non-glial nuclei forming 161 clusters (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T2 neuron atlas generation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%) among T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons comprise 12% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: GABAergic neurons comprise 9% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: Tyraminergic neurons comprise 2.6% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons comprise 1.2% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: Serotonergic neurons comprise 1.2% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: Octopaminergic neurons comprise 0.7% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis.

claim: 12% of T2-derived neurons co-express two or three neurotransmitters.
source: Additionally, 12% of neurons were co-expressing two or three neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter co-expression analysis.

claim: 40% of T2-derived neurons in the atlas were not expressing any neurotransmitter with a log normalized expression <2.
source: The remaining 40% in our atlas were not expressing any neurotransmitter with a log normalized expression <2 (Figure 3H); this is similar to the ratios in the adult midbrain (Croset et al., 2018) and optic lobes (Konstantinides et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3H, with citations to similar findings in other brain regions.

claim: The T2 glial atlas contains 12,315 glial nuclei.
source: We sub-clustered from the T2 atlas for 12,315 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan glial marker repo (Figure 4A; Campbell et al., 1994; Xiong et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T2 glial atlas generation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The T2 glial atlas identified glial cell types: astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, astrocyte-like, and two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial.
source: Similar to our T1+T2 glial atlas, we identified glial cell types: astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, astrocyte-like, and two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial, based on canonical glial makers (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the T2 glial cell type identification analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Chiasm glia were identified in the T2 glial atlas.
source: Interestingly, we identified chiasm glia that may represent the migratory chiasm glia generated from the DL1 lineage (Viktorin et al., 2013; see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the T2 glial atlas with a citation to a previous study about chiasm glia.

claim: The T2 glial atlas contained two female enriched clusters: ensheathing/astrocyte (cluster 7) and chiasm (cluster 5).
source: We found that the T2 glial atlas contained two female enriched clusters: ensheathing/astrocyte (cluster 7) and chiasm (cluster 5), and one male enriched cluster: the astrocyte-like (cluster 3; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-biased cluster analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The T2 glial atlas contained one male enriched cluster: the astrocyte-like (cluster 3).
source: We found that the T2 glial atlas contained two female enriched clusters: ensheathing/astrocyte (cluster 7) and chiasm (cluster 5), and one male enriched cluster: the astrocyte-like (cluster 3; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-biased cluster analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Female glial nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3.
source: We found female nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3 (Figure 5C; Warren et al., 1979).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5C, with a citation supporting these as female-specific genes.

claim: Female glial nuclei were enriched for dsx.
source: Additionally, female nuclei were enriched for dsx (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Male glial nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru.
source: Male glial nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 10; Amrein and Axel, 1997; Meller et al., 1997; Ryner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5C, with citations supporting these as male-specific genes.

claim: 14 neuronal clusters had disproportionate amounts of male and female nuclei.
source: We identified 14 neuronal clusters with disproportionate amounts of male and female nuclei (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-biased cluster analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Female neuronal nuclei expressed higher levels of the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3.
source: Similar to the T2 glia sex differences, we found female nuclei expressed higher levels of the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3 (Figure 5G; Warren et al., 1979).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5G, with a citation supporting these as female-specific genes.

claim: Female neuronal nuclei were enriched for dsx.
source: Additionally, female nuclei were enriched for dsx (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Male neuronal nuclei expressed higher levels of the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru.
source: Male neuronal nuclei expressed higher levels of the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru (Figure 5G; Supplementary file 11; Amrein and Axel, 1997; Meller et al., 1997; Ryner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5G, with citations supporting these as male-specific genes.

claim: The study identified 13 neuropeptides with enriched expression in a limited number of clusters.
source: Among the 49 neuropeptides in Drosophila, we identified 13 with enriched expression in a limited number of clusters, making them suitable as cluster-defining markers (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All neuropeptide-expressing clusters co-express one or more neurotransmitters.
source: We found that all neuropeptide-expressing clusters, co-express one or more neurotransmitters (see Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA.
source: For example, in some cases, one cluster expresses two or more neuropeptide genes (e.g. clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA); conversely, we also observe one neuropeptide expressed in multiple clusters (e.g. Ms, 2 clusters; Tk, 2 clusters; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ms is expressed in 2 clusters.
source: For example, in some cases, one cluster expresses two or more neuropeptide genes (e.g. clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA); conversely, we also observe one neuropeptide expressed in multiple clusters (e.g. Ms, 2 clusters; Tk, 2 clusters; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tk is expressed in 2 clusters.
source: For example, in some cases, one cluster expresses two or more neuropeptide genes (e.g. clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA); conversely, we also observe one neuropeptide expressed in multiple clusters (e.g. Ms, 2 clusters; Tk, 2 clusters; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: T2-derived Ms-2A-LexA-expressing neurons project to multiple layers of the dorsal fan-shaped body and the entire ellipsoid body.
source: However, we found that T2-derived Ms-2A-LexA-expressing neurons project to multiple layers of the dorsal fan-shaped body and the entire ellipsoid body, suggesting an unknown class of Ms+ neurons targeting to EB and/or FB (Figure 6C–C'', Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the morphological analysis of Ms+ neurons shown in Figure 6C-C'' and Video 1.

claim: NPF-2A-lexA and AstA-2A-lexA label neurons with indistinguishable numbers of cells and projections.
source: We found that they were generated at indistinguishable numbers of cells and projections: both had ~20 neurons projecting to a lateral domain of the ellipsoid body and the same two layers of the fan-shaped body (Figure 6D–E; Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the morphological analysis of NPF+ and AstA+ neurons shown in Figures 6D-E and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: High correlations of multiple TFs to each neuropeptide were found.
source: Interestingly, we found high correlations of multiple TFs to each neuropeptide (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most clusters expressed a unique TF combination.
source: We found that most clusters expressed a unique TF combination (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: All zinc-finger TFs are expressed in unique combinatorial codes.
source: This is true for all zinc-finger TFs (Figure 7A) and helix-turn-helix TFs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All helix-turn-helix TFs are expressed in unique combinatorial codes.
source: This is true for all zinc-finger TFs (Figure 7A) and helix-turn-helix TFs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Nearly all clusters expressed a unique combination of homeodomain TFs.
source: Nearly, all clusters expressed a unique combination of homeodomain TFs (Figure 7C), with only a few clusters sharing a homeodomain code (Figure 7C').
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Basic domain, unspecified domain, and high mobility group TFs were more promiscuously expressed.
source: In contrast, basic domain, unspecified domain, and high mobility group TFs were more promiscuously expressed (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: 100% of clusters have unique combinations of zinc finger TF expression (161 unique clusters).
source: Percentage of clusters with unique combinations of TF expression based on TF class zinc finger TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), helix-turn-helix TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), homeodomain TFs = 93.8% (150 unique clusters), basic domain TFs = 69.6% (112 unique clusters), unidentified DNA binding domain TFs = 59% (95 unique clusters), high motility group TFs = 34.2% (55 unique clusters).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the transcription factor combinatorial code analysis.

claim: 100% of clusters have unique combinations of helix-turn-helix TF expression (161 unique clusters).
source: Percentage of clusters with unique combinations of TF expression based on TF class zinc finger TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), helix-turn-helix TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), homeodomain TFs = 93.8% (150 unique clusters), basic domain TFs = 69.6% (112 unique clusters), unidentified DNA binding domain TFs = 59% (95 unique clusters), high motility group TFs = 34.2% (55 unique clusters).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the transcription factor combinatorial code analysis.

claim: 93.8% of clusters have unique combinations of homeodomain TF expression (150 unique clusters).
source: Percentage of clusters with unique combinations of TF expression based on TF class zinc finger TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), helix-turn-helix TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), homeodomain TFs = 93.8% (150 unique clusters), basic domain TFs = 69.6% (112 unique clusters), unidentified DNA binding domain TFs = 59% (95 unique clusters), high motility group TFs = 34.2% (55 unique clusters).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the transcription factor combinatorial code analysis.

claim: 69.6% of clusters have unique combinations of basic domain TF expression (112 unique clusters).

claim: The T1+T2 central brain atlas and T2-specific atlas show similarities including neurons expressing predominantly single fast-acting neurotransmitters.
source: Similarities include neurons expressing predominantly single fast-acting neurotransmitters (discussed below).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and previous scRNA-seq data.

claim: Both T1+T2 and previous datasets show major classes of neurons including MB neurons, olfactory projection neurons, clock neurons, Poxn+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, octopaminergic neurons, corazonergic neurons, and hemocytes.
source: Both datasets show major classes of neurons including MB neurons, olfactory projection neurons, clock neurons, Poxn+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, octopaminergic neurons, corazonergic neurons, and hemocytes.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and previous scRNA-seq data.

claim: The MB neurons that appear in the T2-derived progeny may be due to off-target expression of the Gal4 driver or ambient RNA released during dissociation and sorting.
source: The MB neurons that appear in the T2-derived progeny may be due to off-target expression of our Gal4 driver at stages we have not assayed, or more likely, due to ambient RNA released during the dissociation and sorting steps.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of MB neurons in the T2 atlas.

claim: Fewer distinct neuronal clusters were observed in the T1-derived population (114 clusters) than in the T2-derived neuronal population (161 clusters).
source: Interestingly, we observed fewer distinct neuronal clusters in the T1-derived population (114 clusters; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) than in the T2-derived neuronal population (161 clusters; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between T1 and T2 neuronal cluster numbers.

claim: The T1-derived progeny contain a large population of transcriptionally similar Kenyon cells of the MB.
source: This could be due to the T1-derived progeny containing a large population of transcriptionally similar Kenyon cells of the MB, whereas T2-derived clusters contain fewer, but transcriptionally more diverse, cells than T1-derived progeny.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference in cluster numbers between T1 and T2 populations.

claim: T2-derived clusters contain fewer, but transcriptionally more diverse, cells than T1-derived progeny.
source: This could be due to the T1-derived progeny containing a large population of transcriptionally similar Kenyon cells of the MB, whereas T2-derived clusters contain fewer, but transcriptionally more diverse, cells than T1-derived progeny.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference in cluster numbers between T1 and T2 populations.

claim: Co-expression of neurotransmitters has been reported in other systems.
source: Co-expression of neurotransmitters has been reported in other systems (Granger et al., 2020; Granger et al., 2023; Lozovaya et al., 2018; Meye et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2015; Shabel et al., 2014; Spitzer, 2015; Takács et al., 2018) and it may be biologically relevant in the T2-derived neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies in other systems.

claim: Co-expression of neurotransmitters may be biologically relevant in the T2-derived neurons.
source: Co-expression of neurotransmitters has been reported in other systems (Granger et al., 2020; Granger et al., 2023; Lozovaya et al., 2018; Meye et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2015; Shabel et al., 2014; Spitzer, 2015; Takács et al., 2018) and it may be biologically relevant in the T2-derived neurons.
evidence: This is speculation based on findings in other systems.

claim: It remains unclear if glial clusters with the same cell type annotation represent distinct glial identities or different transcriptional states within these populations.
source: It remains unclear if these clusters with the same cell type annotation represent distinct glial identities or different transcriptional states within these populations.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the interpretation of multiple clusters with the same glial subtype annotation.

claim: The lack of differential gene expression between T1- and T2-derived glia suggests these cell types are similar despite different developmental origins.
source: The lack of differential gene expression between T1- and T2-derived glia suggests these cell types are similar despite different developmental origins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differential gene expression between T1 and T2 glia.

claim: The T2 glia atlas contains more clusters than the T1+T2 atlas due to nearly 4x the number of glia captured.
source: The T2 glia atlas contains more clusters than the T1+T2 atlas that may be due to the nearly 4x the number of glia captured (T1+T2 atlas 3,409 nuclei; T2 atlas – 12,315 nuclei).
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in the number of glial nuclei captured.

claim: Chiasm glia have been shown to be derived from the T2 lineage DL1 and migrate into the optic lobe.
source: Additionally, we captured chiasm glia that have been shown to be derived from the T2 lineage DL1 and migrate into the optic lobe (Viktorin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The chiasm glia nuclei could represent either chiasm glia that did not migrate out of the central brain or optic lobe tissue that was not completely removed during dissections.
source: These nuclei could represent either chiasm glia that did not migrate out of the central brain or optic lobe tissue that was not completely removed during dissections.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of chiasm glia in the T2 atlas.

claim: Sex-specific genes may reflect sex-specific differences in the adult central brain and may provide insight into how behavioral circuits are linked to sex-specific behaviors.
source: These genes may reflect sex-specific differences in the adult central brain and may provide insight into how behavioral circuits are linked to sex-specific behaviors.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of sex-specific gene expression.

claim: Zinc finger TFs and homeodomain TFs form combinatorial codes specific for distinct cell types.
source: Our atlas showed zinc finger TFs and homeodomain TFs as forming combinatorial codes specific for distinct cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor expression analysis.

claim: TF combinations may determine neuronal functional properties by establishing and maintaining neuronal identities.
source: This raises the possibility that these TF combinations determine neuronal functional properties, by establishing and maintaining neuronal identities.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of TF combinatorial codes.

claim: The finding of more zinc finger TFs expressed in unique combinatorial codes compared to homeodomain TFs may be a caution to focusing too narrowly on homeodomain TFs function.
source: Interestingly, we found more zinc finger TFs expressed in unique combinatorial codes compared to homeodomain TFs; this may be a caution to focusing too narrowly on homeodomain TFs function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data suggesting a broader focus on TF classes.

claim: The current sparse TF expression patterns may be due, in part, to false negative results due to low read depths.
source: It is also possible that the current sparse TF expression patterns are due, in part, to false negative results due to low read depths.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential technical limitation of the study.

claim: Increasing read depth or performing functional assays can resolve potential false negative results in TF expression.
source: This can be resolved by increasing read depth or by performing functional assays.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work to address potential limitations.
